image.alt: A cow standing on the ground is shown with boxes marked on the legs, head, and knees. Inside the head box markings are shown. A surveillance system is shown beside the cow image.

section.heading: Chapter 6
Orthogonality and Least Squares

note.title: Introductory Example
note.heading: Introductory Example
Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
note.paragraph: Meet BETSY, the Bovine Expert Tracking and Surveillance system developed by OneCup AI. BETSY helps ranchers keep a virtual eye on their cattle at all times.

Geoffrey Shmigelsky, an Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning specialist, sparked a transformative idea while sitting around a campfire at a family reunion. He asked Mokah Shmigelsky’s rancher cousins what they wanted AI to do for them, and the response was simple—identify each of our cows. This initial idea blossomed into BETSY, a sophisticated system that now monitors the health and wellness of cattle across the prairies of Canada and beyond.

BETSY’s monitoring process is thorough and detailed, providing ranchers with a sense of reassurance. Her “brain” is divided into levels. Ranchers install cameras to record digital videos of their herds, which are sent in real-time to BETSY’s computer system. In Level 1, BETSY draws a bounding box around each animal. Moving into Level 2, she identifies key points such as the animal's eyes, nose, hips, knees, hooves, and tail. By Level 3, she can identify which animal from the herd is in each specific box. She then monitors the animal’s behavior in Level 4. The first clue that something is amiss with an animal is a change in behavior. Level 5 involves analyzing the animal’s behavior over time and alerting the rancher to any significant differences that appear. By tracking the animal’s behavior, BETSY can detect changes in feeding, movement, or body stance, which may indicate that an animal is sick and needs care. BETSY sends an alert to the rancher’s cell phone if an animal shows signs of illness, shows up lame, or if a cow is going into labor and may need assistance as she delivers her calf.

image.alt: A diagram of BETSY’s monitoring process is shown.

note.paragraph: OneCup AI, responding to client requests and drawing from its own expertise, continues to enhance BETSY by teaching her new skills. But how does BETSY learn? She learns by watching training videos. During this supervised learning process, BETSY builds a model that is consistent with the information in the videos she has been given. For instance, BETSY watched videos to distinguish between cows in labor and those not in labor. This continuous learning process, which ensures that BETSY constantly improves and adapts to new challenges, instills confidence in her capabilities.

BETSY’s success is only as good as the data she is trained on. One of the more challenging programs inside BETSY involves deciding whether the animal in a photo or video is a cow, horse, sheep, or goat. When an Alberta Clipper blanketed the prairies (and animals) with white snow, BETSY suddenly identified a lot more “sheep” than she had the day before! Once BETSY had her training videos updated to include correctly identified animals covered in snow, she was no longer fooled by a few flakes.

Why stop at cattle on the prairies of Canada? One of the most useful features of mathematical techniques is that, once they have been developed, they are independent of their motivational source. The methods developed by OneCup AI to monitor cattle can be adapted to monitor other animals. For example, BETSY now has programs for monitoring the health and well-being of horses, sheep, pigs, cats, and dogs. Geoffrey and Mokah Shmigelsky are even talking to wildlife specialists in the Amazon, discussing the potential for BETSY to help monitor the health and wellness of wildlife living in the rainforest.

image.alt: The identification of a bird, a cow, and an octopus using A I.

note.paragraph: According to Geoffrey, “At OneCup AI, we love linear algebra!” Like is done at OneCup AI, machine learning and AI comprise developing systems that interpret external data correctly, learn from such data, and use that learning to achieve specific goals and tasks through flexibility and adaptation. The foundational ideas for everything from digital video feeds to Deep Learning depend on linear algebra. In Section 6.2, we see a simple way to design a matrix so that matrix multiplication can identify a specified pattern of blue and white squares. In Sections 6.5, 6.6, and 6.8, we explore techniques used in machine learning.

section.paragraph: Solving systems of equations has been a common theme throughout this text, but what happens when there are no solutions? A good approximation to a solution may still be enough to make sound decisions. A well-defined notion of nearness is needed to find an approximate solution to an inconsistent system of equations. Although the measure of “nearness” may change depending on the application, one notion of distance is introduced in Section 6.1, along with the notion of orthogonality. As illustrated in Sections 6.2 and 6.3, orthogonality can be used to simplify calculations and to identify the nearest point in a subspace $$W$$ to a specified point outside of $$W$$ . By taking $$W$$ to be the column space of a matrix, in Section 6.5, a method for producing approximate (least-squares) solutions for inconsistent linear systems is developed, providing an essential technique in Machine Learning, which is discussed in Sections 6.6 and 6.8. Section 6.4 provides another opportunity to see orthogonal projections at work, presenting a matrix factorization widely used in numerical linear algebra. A more abstract view of orthogonality is given in Section 6.7, providing the flexibility needed to tailor the measure of “nearness” to the application.
section.heading: 6.1 Inner Product, Length, and Orthogonality
section.paragraph: Geometric concepts of length, distance, and perpendicularity, which are well known for $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ and $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , are defined here for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . These concepts provide powerful geometric tools for solving many applied problems, including the least-squares problems mentioned above. All three notions are defined in terms of the inner product of two vectors.
section.heading: The Inner Product
section.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then we regard $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ as $$n \times 1$$ matrices. The transpose $$\mathbf{u}^{T}$$ is a $$1 \times n$$ matrix, and the matrix product $$\mathbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{v}$$ is a $$1 \times 1$$ matrix, which we write as a single real number (a scalar) without brackets. The number $$\mathbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{v}$$ is called the inner product of $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and often it is written as $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}$$ . This inner product, mentioned in the exercises for Section 2.1, is also referred to as a dot product. If
$$\mathbf{u} = \left[\right. u_{1} u_{2} \vdots u_{n} \left]\right. \text{and} \mathbf{v} = \left[\right. v_{1} v_{2} \vdots v_{n} \left]\right.$$
then the inner product of $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ is

$$\boxed{[ \begin{matrix}u_{1} & u_{2} & \hdots & u_{n} \end{matrix} ] \left[\right. \begin{matrix}v_{1} \\ v_{2} \\ \vdots \\ v_{n}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = u_{1} v_{1} + u_{2} v_{2} + \hdots + u_{n} v_{n}}$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Compute $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}$$ and $$\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}$$ for $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 5} \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 2 \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} & = & \mathbf{u}^{T} \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}2 & - 5 & - 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 2 \\ - 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left(2\right) \left(3\right) + \left(- 5\right) \left(2\right) + \left(- 1\right) \left(- 3\right) = - 1 \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u} & = & \mathbf{v}^{T} \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}3 & 2 & - 3\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ - 5 \\ - 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left(3\right) \left(2\right) + \left(2\right) \left(- 5\right) + \left(- 3\right) \left(- 1\right) = - 1$$

section.paragraph: It is clear from the calculations in Example 1 why $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}$$ . This commutativity of the inner product holds in general. The following properties of the inner product are easily deduced from properties of the transpose operation in Section 2.1. (See Exercises 29 and 30 at the end of this section.)

note.title: Theorem 1
note.heading: Theorem 1
note.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and $$\textbf{w}$$ be vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , and let $$c$$ be a scalar. Then

list.item: $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}$$
$$( \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} ) \cdot \textbf{w} = \mathbf{u} \cdot \textbf{w} + \mathbf{v} \cdot \textbf{w}$$
$$( c \mathbf{u} ) \cdot \mathbf{v} = c ( \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} ) = \mathbf{u} \cdot ( c \mathbf{v} )$$
$$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u} \geq 0$$ , and $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0$$ if and only if $$\mathbf{u} = \textbf{0}$$

section.paragraph: Properties (b) and (c) can be combined several times to produce the following useful rule:
$$\boxed{( c_{1} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{u}_{p} ) \cdot \textbf{w} = c_{1} ( \mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \textbf{w}) + \hdots + c_{p} ( \mathbf{u}_{p} \cdot \textbf{w})}$$
section.heading: The Length of a Vector
section.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{v}$$ is in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , with entries $$v_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$v_{n}$$ , then the square root of $$\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}$$ is defined because $$\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}$$ is nonnegative.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The length (or norm) of $$\mathbf{v}$$ is the nonnegative scalar $$\parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel$$ defined by

$$\parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel = \sqrt{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}} = \sqrt{v_{1}^{2} + v_{2}^{2} + \hdots + v_{n}^{2}} , \text{and} \parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel^{2} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}$$

section.paragraph: Suppose $$\mathbf{v}$$ is in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , say, $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} a \\ b \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . If we identify $$\mathbf{v}$$ with a geometric point in the plane, as usual, then $$\parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel$$ coincides with the standard notion of the length of the line segment from the origin to $$\mathbf{v}.$$ This follows from the Pythagorean Theorem applied to a triangle such as the one in Figure 1.

image.alt: A graph shows a right-angled triangle lying in the second quadrant with one of its vertices on the origin.

figure.caption: Figure 1 Interpretation of ∥v∥ ﻿as length

section.paragraph: A similar calculation with the diagonal of a rectangular box shows that the definition of length of a vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ coincides with the usual notion of length.
For any scalar $$c$$ , the length of $$c\mathbf{v}$$ is $$|c|$$ times the length of $$\mathbf{v}$$ . That is,
$$\boxed{\parallel \textit{c} \textbf{v} \parallel = \left|\right. c \left|\right. \parallel \textbf{v} \parallel}$$

(To see this, compute $$\text{∥} \textit{c}\textbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2} = (c\mathbf{v}) \cdot (c\mathbf{v}) = c^{2}\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} = c^{2} \text{∥} \textbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2}$$ and take square roots.)

A vector whose length is $$1$$ is called a unit vector. If we divide a nonzero vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ by its length—that is, multiply by $$1/ \text{∥} \textbf{v} \text{∥}$$ —we obtain a unit vector $$\mathbf{u}$$ because the length of $$\mathbf{u}$$ is $$\left( 1/ \text{∥} \textbf{v} \text{∥} \right) \text{∥} \textbf{v} \text{∥}$$ . The process of creating $$\mathbf{u}$$ from $$\mathbf{v}$$ is sometimes called normalizing $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and we say that $$\mathbf{u}$$ is in the same direction as $$\mathbf{v}$$ .
Several examples that follow use the space-saving notation for (column) vectors.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{v} = (1, - 2,2,0)$$ . Find a unit vector $$\mathbf{u}$$ in the same direction as $$\mathbf{v}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: First, compute the length of $$\mathbf{v}$$ :

$$\parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel^{2} & = & \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \left(( 1 )\right)^{2} + \left(\left(\right. - 2 \left.\right)\right)^{2} + \left(( 2 )\right)^{2} + \left(0\right)^{2} = 9 \parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel & = & \sqrt{9} = 3$$
Then, multiply $$\mathbf{v}$$ by $$1/ \text{∥} \textbf{v} \text{∥}$$ to obtain
$$\mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{\parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel} \mathbf{v} = \frac{1}{3} \mathbf{v} = \frac{1}{3} \left[\right. 1 - 2 2 0 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 1 / 3 - 2 / 3 2 / 3 0 \left]\right.$$
To check that $$\text{∥} \textbf{u} \text{∥} = 1$$ , it suffices to show that $$\text{∥} \textbf{u} \text{∥} ^{2} = 1$$ .

$$\parallel \mathbf{u} \parallel^{2} & = & \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u} = \left(\left(\right. \frac{1}{3} \left.\right)\right)^{2} + \left(\left(\right. - \frac{2}{3} \left.\right)\right)^{2} + \left(\left(\right. \frac{2}{3} \left.\right)\right)^{2} + \left(( 0 )\right)^{2} & = & \frac{1}{9} + \frac{4}{9} + \frac{4}{9} + 0 = 1$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Let $$W$$ be the subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ spanned by $$\textbf{x} = \left( \frac{2}{3} \text{,} 1 \right)$$ . Find a unit vector $$\textbf{z}$$ that is a basis for $$W$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: $$W$$ consists of all multiples of $$\textbf{x}$$ , as in Figure 2(a). Any nonzero vector in $$W$$ is a basis for $$W$$ . To simplify the calculation, “scale” $$\textbf{x}$$ to eliminate fractions. That is, multiply $$\textbf{x}$$ by $$3$$ to get
$$\textbf{y} = \left[\right. 2 3 \left]\right.$$

image.alt: A graph shows the normalization of a vector with a straight line passing through the origin.

figure.caption: Figure 2﻿ ﻿Normalizing a vector to produce a unit vector.

image.alt: A graph shows an equivalent vector and a unit vector spanning W.

example.paragraph: Now compute $$\text{∥} \textbf{y} \text{∥} ^{2} = 2^{2} + 3^{2} = 13$$ , $$\text{∥} \textbf{y} \text{∥} = \sqrt{13}$$ , and normalize $$\textbf{y}$$ to get
$$\textbf{z} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \left[\right. 2 3 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 2 / \sqrt{13} 3 / \sqrt{13} \left]\right.$$
See Figure 2(b). Another unit vector is $$\left( - 2/\sqrt{13} \text{,} - 3/\sqrt{13} \right)$$ .

section.heading: Distance in ℝn
section.paragraph: We are ready now to describe how close one vector is to another. Recall that if $$a$$ and $$b$$ are real numbers, the distance on the number line between $$a$$ and $$b$$ is the number $$|a - b|$$ . Two examples are shown in Figure 3. This definition of distance in $$\mathbb{R}$$ has a direct analogue in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

image.alt: Two number lines depict the horizontal distance between points a and b.

figure.caption: Figure 3 Distances in ℝ

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: For $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the distance between $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ , written as $$\text{dist} \left( \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \right)$$ , is the length of the vector $$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$$ . That is,
$$\text{dist} ( \mathbf{u} , \mathbf{v} ) = \parallel \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \parallel$$

section.paragraph: In $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ and $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , this definition of distance coincides with the usual formulas for the Euclidean distance between two points, as the next two examples show.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Compute the distance between the vectors $$\mathbf{u} = \left( 7 \text{,} 1 \right)$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = \left( 3 \text{,} 2 \right)$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Calculate

$$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}7 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. - \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}4 \\ - 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. \parallel \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \parallel & = & \sqrt{4^{2} + \left(\right. - 1 \left.\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{17}$$

The vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and $$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$$ are shown in Figure 4. When the vector $$\textbf{u } - \mathbf{v}$$ is added to $$\mathbf{v}$$ , the result is $$\mathbf{u}$$ . Notice that the parallelogram in Figure 4 shows that the distance from $$\mathbf{u}$$ to $$\mathbf{v}$$ is the same as the distance from $$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$$ to $$\textbf{0}$$ .

image.alt: A graph shows two straight lines and a rhombus with unit 1 marked on both axes.

figure.caption: Figure 4 The distance between u ﻿and v ﻿is the length of u−v

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{u} = \left( u_{1} \text{,} u_{2} \text{,} u_{3} \right)$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = \left( v_{1} \text{,} v_{2} \text{,} v_{3} \right)$$ , then

$$\text{dist} \left(\right. \mathbf{u} , \mathbf{v} \left.\right) & = & \parallel \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \parallel = \sqrt{( \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} ) \cdot ( \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} )} & = & \sqrt{\left(\right. u_{1} - v_{1} \left.\right)^{2} + \left(\right. u_{2} - v_{2} \left.\right)^{2} + \left(\right. u_{3} - v_{3} \left.\right)^{2}}$$

section.heading: Orthogonal Vectors
section.paragraph: The rest of this chapter depends on the fact that the concept of perpendicular lines in ordinary Euclidean geometry has an analogue in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

Consider $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ or $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ and two lines through the origin determined by vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ . The two lines shown in Figure 5 are geometrically perpendicular if and only if the distance from $$\mathbf{u}$$ to $$\mathbf{v}$$ is the same as the distance from $$\mathbf{u}$$ to $$- \mathbf{v}$$ . This is the same as requiring the squares of the distances to be the same. Now

$$\left(\left[\right. \text{dist} \left(\right. \mathbf{u} , - \mathbf{v} \left.\right) \left]\right.\right)^{2} & = & \parallel \mathbf{u} - \left(- \mathbf{v}\right) \parallel^{2} = \parallel \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \parallel^{2} & & = & ( \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} ) \cdot ( \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} ) & & = & \mathbf{u} \cdot ( \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} ) + \mathbf{v} \cdot ( \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} ) & \text{Theorem} 1 \left(\right. \text{b} \left.\right) & = & \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} & \text{Theorem} 1 \left(\right. \text{a} \left.\right) , \left(\right. \text{b} \left.\right) & = & \parallel \textbf{u} \parallel^{2} + \parallel \textbf{v} \parallel^{2} + 2 \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} & \text{Theorem} 1 \left(\right. \text{a} \left.\right)$$

image.alt: A figure shows vectors u, v, and negative v as the three vertices of a triangle.

figure.caption: Figure 5

section.paragraph: The same calculations with $$\mathbf{v}$$ and $$- \mathbf{v}$$ interchanged show that

$$\left[\right. \text{dist} ( \mathbf{u} , \mathbf{v} ) \left]\right.^{2} & = & \parallel \textbf{u} \parallel^{2} + \parallel - \mathbf{v} \parallel^{2} + 2 \mathbf{u} \cdot \left(\right. - \mathbf{v} \left.\right) & = & \parallel \textbf{u} \parallel^{2} + \parallel \textbf{v} \parallel^{2} - 2 \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}$$
The two squared distances are equal if and only if $$2\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = - 2\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}$$ , which happens if and only if $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$$ .

This calculation shows that when vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are identified with geometric points, the corresponding lines through the points and the origin are perpendicular if and only if $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$$ . The following definition generalizes to $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ this notion of perpendicularity (or orthogonality, as it is commonly called in linear algebra).

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Two vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ are orthogonal (to each other) if $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$$ .

section.paragraph: Observe that the zero vector is orthogonal to every vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ because $$\textbf{0}^{T}\mathbf{v} = 0$$ for all $$\mathbf{v}$$ .

The next theorem provides a useful fact about orthogonal vectors. The proof follows immediately from the calculation in (1) and the definition of orthogonality. The right triangle shown in Figure 6 provides a visualization of the lengths that appear in the theorem.

image.alt: A figure shows a tilted right-angled triangle and line segment meeting one of the triangle's vertices at point 0.

figure.caption: Figure 6

note.title: Theorem 2
note.heading: Theorem 2
The Pythagorean Theorem
note.paragraph: Two vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are orthogonal if and only if $$\text{∥} \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2} = \text{∥} \textbf{u} \text{∥} ^{2} + \text{∥} \textbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2}$$ .

section.heading: Orthogonal Complements
section.paragraph: To provide practice using inner products, we introduce a concept here that will be of use in Section 6.3 and elsewhere in the chapter. If a vector $$\textbf{z}$$ is orthogonal to every vector in a subspace $$W$$ of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then $$\textbf{z}$$ is said to be orthogonal to $$W$$ . The set of all vectors $$\textbf{z}$$ that are orthogonal to $$W$$ is called the orthogonal complement of $$W$$ and is denoted by $$W^{\bot}$$ (and read as “ $$W$$ perpendicular” or simply “ $$W$$ perp”).

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Let $$W$$ be a plane through the origin in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , and let $$L$$ be the line through the origin and perpendicular to $$W$$ . If $$\textbf{z}$$ and $$\textbf{w}$$ are nonzero, $$\textbf{z}$$ is on $$L$$ , and $$\textbf{w}$$ is in $$W$$ , then the line segment from $$0$$ to $$\textbf{z}$$ is perpendicular to the line segment from $$0$$ to $$\textbf{w}$$ ; that is, $$\textbf{z} \cdot \textbf{w} = 0$$ . See Figure 7. So each vector on $$L$$ is orthogonal to every $$\textbf{w}$$ in $$W$$ . In fact, $$L$$ consists of all vectors that are orthogonal to the $$\textbf{w}$$ ’s in $$W$$ , and $$W$$ consists of all vectors orthogonal to the $$\textbf{z} \text{’s}$$ in $$L$$ . That is,
$$L = W^{\bot} \text{and} W = L^{\bot}$$

image.alt: A figure shows a plane denoted by uppercase W and a straight line passing perpendicularly through the midpoint 0 in the plane.

figure.caption: Figure 7 A plane and line through 0 ﻿as orthogonal complements

section.paragraph: The following two facts about $$W^{\bot}$$ , with $$W$$ a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , are needed later in the chapter. Proofs are suggested in Exercises 37 and 38. Exercises 35–39 provide excellent practice using properties of the inner product.

list.item: A vector $$\textbf{x}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ if and only if $$\textbf{x}$$ is orthogonal to every vector in a set that spans $$W$$ .
$$W^{\bot}$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

section.paragraph: The next theorem and Exercise 39 verify the claims made in Section 4.5 concerning the subspaces shown in Figure 8.

image.alt: A figure shows the fundamental subspaces of matrix A represented as two planes and two lines passing through each plane.

figure.caption: Figure 8 The fundamental subspaces determined by an m×n ﻿matrix A

section.paragraph: Remark: A common way to prove that two sets, say $$S$$ and $$T$$ , are equal is to show that $$S$$ is a subset of $$T$$ and $$T$$ is a subset of $$S$$ . The proof of the next theorem that $$\text{Nul} A = \left( \text{Row} A \right)^{\bot}$$ is established by showing that $$\text{Nul} A$$ is a subset of $$\left( \text{Row} A \right)^{\bot}$$ and $$\left( \text{Row} A \right)^{\bot}$$ is a subset of $$\text{Nul} A$$ . That is, an arbitrary element $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\text{Nul} A$$ is shown to be in $$\left( \text{Row} A \right)^{\bot}$$ , and then an arbitrary element $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\left( \text{Row} A \right)^{\bot}$$ is shown to be in $$\text{Nul} A$$ .

note.title: Theorem 3
note.heading: Theorem 3
note.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be an $$m \times n$$ matrix. The orthogonal complement of the row space of $$A$$ is the null space of $$A$$ , and the orthogonal complement of the column space of $$A$$ is the null space of $$A^{T}$$ :
$$\left( \text{Row} A\right)^{\bot} = \text{Nul} A \text{and} \left( \text{Col} A\right)^{\bot} = \text{Nul} A^{T}$$

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: The row–column rule for computing $$A\textbf{x}$$ shows that if $$\textbf{x}$$ is in $$\text{Nul} A$$ , then $$\textbf{x}$$ is orthogonal to each row of $$A$$ (with the rows treated as vectors in $$\left. \mathbb{R}^{n} \right)$$ . Since the rows of $$A$$ span the row space, $$\textbf{x}$$ is orthogonal to $$\text{Row} A$$ . Conversely, if $$\textbf{x}$$ is orthogonal to $$\text{Row} A$$ , then $$\textbf{x}$$ is certainly orthogonal to each row of $$A$$ , and hence $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ . This proves the first statement of the theorem. Since this statement is true for any matrix, it is true for $$A^{T}$$ . That is, the orthogonal complement of the row space of $$A^{T}$$ is the null space of $$A^{T}$$ . This proves the second statement, because $$\text{Row} A^{T} = \text{Col} A$$ .
section.heading: Angles in ℝ2 and ℝ3 (Optional)
section.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are nonzero vectors in either $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ or $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , then there is a nice connection between their inner product and the angle $$\vartheta$$ between the two line segments from the origin to the points identified with $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ . The formula is
$$\boxed{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \parallel \mathbf{u} \parallel\parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel \cos \vartheta}$$

To verify this formula for vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , consider the triangle shown in Figure 9, with sides of lengths $$\parallel \mathbf{u} \parallel$$ , $$\parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel$$ , and $$\parallel \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \parallel$$ . By the law of cosines,

$$\parallel \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \parallel^{2} = \parallel \textbf{u} \parallel^{2} + \parallel \textbf{v} \parallel^{2} - 2 \parallel \textbf{u} \parallel \parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel\cos \vartheta$$

image.alt: A graph shows an inverted scalene triangle lying in the first and the second quadrant with one of its vertices on the origin.

figure.caption: Figure 9 The angle between two vectors

section.paragraph: which can be rearranged to produce

problem.paragraph: If $$W \neq \left\{ \textbf{0} \right\}$$ , let $$\left\{ \textbf{b}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \textbf{b}_{p} \right\}$$ be a basis for $$W$$ , where $$1 \leq p \leq n$$ . Let $$A$$ be the $$p \times n$$ matrix having rows $$\textbf{b}_{1}^{T}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\textbf{b}_{p}^{T}$$ . It follows that $$W$$ is the row space of $$A$$ . Theorem 3 implies that $$W^{\bot} = \left( \text{Row} A)^{\bot} = \text{Nul} A \right.$$ and hence $$\text{dim} W^{\bot} = \text{dim} \text{Nul} A$$ . Thus, $$\text{dim} W + \text{dim} W^{\bot} = \text{dim Row} A + \text{dim Nul} A = \text{rank} A + \text{dim Nul} A = n$$ , by the Rank Theorem. If $$W = \left\{ \textbf{0} \right\}$$ , then $$W^{\bot} = \mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , and the result follows.

section.heading: 6.2 Orthogonal Sets
section.paragraph: A set of vectors $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is said to be an orthogonal set if each pair of distinct vectors from the set is orthogonal, that is, if $$\mathbf{u}_{i} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{j} = 0$$ whenever $$i \neq j$$ .

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Show that $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{3} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal set, where
$$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left[\right. 3 1 1 \left]\right. , \mathbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. - 1 2 1 \left]\right. , \mathbf{u}_{3} = \left[\right. - 1 / 2 - 2 7 / 2 \left]\right.$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Consider the three possible pairs of distinct vectors, namely $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ , $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{3} \right\}$$ , and $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{3} \right\}$$ .

$$\mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2} & = & 3 \left(\right. - 1 \left.\right) + 1 \left(\right. 2 \left.\right) + 1 \left(\right. 1 \left.\right) = 0 \mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{3} & = & 3 \left(\right. - \frac{1}{2} \left.\right) + 1 \left(\right. - 2 \left.\right) + 1 \left(\right. \frac{7}{2} \left.\right) = 0 \mathbf{u}_{2} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{3} & = & - 1 \left(\right. - \frac{1}{2} \left.\right) + 2 \left(\right. - 2 \left.\right) + 1 \left(\right. \frac{7}{2} \left.\right) = 0$$

Each pair of distinct vectors is orthogonal, and so $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{3} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal set. See Figure 1; the three line segments are mutually perpendicular.

note.title: Theorem ﻿4
note.heading: Theorem ﻿4
note.paragraph: If $$S = \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then $$S$$ is linearly independent and hence is a basis for the subspace spanned by $$S$$ .

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: If $$\textbf{0} = c_{1}\mathbf{u}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}\mathbf{u}_{p}$$ for some scalars $$c_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$c_{p}$$ , then

$$0 & = & \textbf{0} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} = ( c_{1} \mathbf{u}_{1} + c_{2} \mathbf{u}_{2} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{u}_{p} ) \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} & = & ( c_{1} \mathbf{u}_{1} ) \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} + ( c_{2} \mathbf{u}_{2} ) \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} + \hdots + ( c_{p} \mathbf{u}_{p} ) \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} & = & c_{1} ( \mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} ) + c_{2} ( \mathbf{u}_{2} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} ) + \hdots + c_{p} ( \mathbf{u}_{p} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} ) & = & c_{1} ( \mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} )$$

because $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ is orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{p}$$ . Since $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ is nonzero, $$\mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}$$ is not zero and so $$c_{1} = 0$$ . Similarly, $$c_{2}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$c_{p}$$ must be zero. Thus $$S$$ is linearly independent.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: An orthogonal basis for a subspace $$W$$ of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a basis for $$W$$ that is also an orthogonal set.

section.paragraph: The next theorem suggests why an orthogonal basis is much nicer than other bases. The weights in a linear combination can be computed easily.

note.title: Theorem ﻿5﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿5﻿
note.paragraph: Let $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ be an orthogonal basis for a subspace $$W$$ of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . For each $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$W$$ , the weights in the linear combination
$$\textbf{y} = c_{1} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{u}_{p}$$
are given by
$$c_{j} = \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{j}}{\mathbf{u}_{j} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{j}} \left(j = 1 , \ldots , p\right)$$

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: As in the preceding proof, the orthogonality of $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ shows that
$$\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} = ( c_{1} \mathbf{u}_{1} + c_{2} \mathbf{u}_{2} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{u}_{p} ) \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} = c_{1} ( \mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} )$$

Since $$\mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}$$ is not zero, the equation above can be solved for $$c_{1}$$ . To find $$c_{j}$$ for $$j = 2$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$p$$ , compute $$\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{j}$$ and solve for $$c_{j}$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: The set $$S = \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{3} \right\}$$ in Example 1 is an orthogonal basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . Express the vector $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 6 \\ 1 \\ {- 8} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ as a linear combination of the vectors in $$S$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Compute

$$\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} & = & 11 , & \textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2} & = & - 12 , & \textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{3} & = & - 33 \mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} & = & 11 , & \mathbf{u}_{2} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2} & = & 6 , & \mathbf{u}_{3} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{3} & = & 33 / 2$$
By Theorem 5,

$$\textbf{y} & = & \frac{\left(\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}\right)_{1}}{\mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \frac{\textbf{y}\cdot\textbf{u}_{2}}{\mathbf{u}_{2} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2}} \mathbf{u}_{2} + \frac{\left(\mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}\right)_{3}}{\mathbf{u}_{3} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{3}} \mathbf{u}_{3} & = & \frac{11}{11} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \frac{- 12}{6} \mathbf{u}_{2} + \frac{- 33}{33 / 2} \mathbf{u}_{3} & = & \mathbf{u}_{1} - 2 \mathbf{u}_{2} - 2 \mathbf{u}_{3}$$

section.paragraph: Notice how easy it is to compute the weights needed to build $$\textbf{y}$$ from an orthogonal basis. If the basis were not orthogonal, it would be necessary to solve a system of linear equations in order to find the weights, as in Chapter 1.
We turn next to a construction that will become a key step in many calculations involving orthogonality, and it will lead to a geometric interpretation of Theorem 5.
section.heading: An Orthogonal Projection
section.paragraph: Given a nonzero vector $$\mathbf{u}$$ in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , consider the problem of decomposing a vector $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ into the sum of two vectors, one a multiple of $$\mathbf{u}$$ and the other orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}$$ . We wish to write
$$\textbf{y} = \hat{\textbf{y}} + \textbf{z}$$

where $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} = \alpha\mathbf{u}$$ for some scalar $$\alpha$$ and $$\textbf{z}$$ is some vector orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}$$ . See Figure 2. Given any scalar $$\alpha$$ , let $$\textbf{z} = \textbf{y} - \alpha\mathbf{u}$$ , so that (1) is satisfied. Then $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}$$ if and only if
$$0 = ( \textbf{y} - \alpha \mathbf{u} ) \cdot \mathbf{u} = \textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u} - ( \alpha \mathbf{u} ) \cdot \mathbf{u} = \textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u} - \alpha ( \textbf{u}\cdot\textbf{u} )$$

image.alt: A figure shows a horizontal plane W with three vectors originating from point 0 on the plane.

figure.caption: Figure 2 Finding α to make ﻿ y−yˆ ﻿orthogonal to u

section.paragraph: That is, (1) is satisfied with $$\textbf{z}$$ orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}$$ if and only if $$\alpha = \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}}$$ and $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} = \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}$$ . The vector $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is called the orthogonal projection of ﻿ $$\mathbf{y}$$ onto $$\mathbf{u}$$ , and the vector $$\textbf{z}$$ is called the component of $$\mathbf{y}$$ orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}$$ .

If $$c$$ is any nonzero scalar and if $$\mathbf{u}$$ is replaced by $$c\mathbf{u}$$ in the definition of $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ , then the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$c\mathbf{u}$$ is exactly the same as the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$\mathbf{u}$$ (Exercise 39). Hence this projection is determined by the subspace $$L$$ spanned by $$\mathbf{u}$$ (the line through $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$0$$ ). Sometimes $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is denoted by $$\text{proj} _{L}\textbf{y}$$ and is called the orthogonal projection of $$\mathbf{y}$$ onto $$L$$ . That is,
$$\boxed{\hat{\textbf{y}} = \text{proj} _{L} \textbf{y} = \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}} \mathbf{u}}$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 7 \\ 6 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 4 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Find the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$\mathbf{u}$$ . Then write $$\textbf{y}$$ as the sum of two orthogonal vectors, one in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u} \right\}$$ and one orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Compute

$$\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}7 \\ 6\end{matrix} \left]\right. \cdot \left[\right. \begin{matrix}4 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. = 40 \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}4 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. \cdot \left[\right. \begin{matrix}4 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. = 20$$
The orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$\mathbf{u}$$ is
$$\hat{\textbf{y}} = \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}} \mathbf{u} = \frac{40}{20} \mathbf{u} = 2 \left[\right. 4 2 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 8 4 \left]\right.$$
and the component of $$\textbf{y}$$ orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}$$ is
$$\textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} = \left[\right. 7 6 \left]\right. - \left[\right. 8 4 \left]\right. = \left[\right. - 1 2 \left]\right.$$
The sum of these two vectors is $$\textbf{y}$$ . That is,

$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}7 \\ 6\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}8 \\ 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. & + & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. \uparrow & & \uparrow & & \uparrow \mathbf{y} & & \hat{\mathbf{y}} & & \left(\right. \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}} \left.\right)$$

This decomposition of $$\textbf{y}$$ is illustrated in Figure 3. Note: If the calculations above are correct, then $$\left\{ \widehat{\textbf{y}} \text{,} \textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}} \right\}$$ will be an orthogonal set. As a check, compute
$$\hat{\textbf{y}} \cdot \left(\textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}}\right) = \left[\right. 8 4 \left]\right. \cdot \left[\right. - 1 2 \left]\right. = - 8 + 8 = 0$$

image.alt: A graph shows the orthogonal projection of a vector represented as y onto a line L that passes through the origin.

figure.caption: Figure 3 The orthogonal projection of y onto ﻿a line L through the origin.

section.paragraph: Since the line segment in Figure 3 between $$\textbf{y}$$ and $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is perpendicular to $$L$$ , by construction of $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ , the point identified with $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is the closest point of $$L$$ to $$\textbf{y}$$ . (This can be proved from geometry. We will assume this for $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ now and prove it for $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ in Section 6.3.)

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the distance in Figure 3 from $$\textbf{y}$$ to $$L$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to $$L$$ is the length of the perpendicular line segment from $$\textbf{y}$$ to the orthogonal projection $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ . This length equals the length of $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ . Thus the distance is
$$\parallel \textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} \parallel = \sqrt{\left(\left(\right. - 1 \left.\right)\right)^{2} + 2^{2}} = \sqrt{5}$$

section.heading: A Geometric Interpretation of Theorem 5
section.paragraph: The formula for the orthogonal projection $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ in (2) has the same appearance as each of the terms in Theorem 5. Thus Theorem 5 decomposes a vector $$\textbf{y}$$ into a sum of orthogonal projections onto one-dimensional subspaces.

It is easy to visualize the case in which $$W = \mathbb{R}^{2} = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ , with $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ orthogonal. Any $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ can be written in the form

$$\textbf{y} = \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}}{\mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2}}{\mathbf{u}_{2} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2}} \mathbf{u}_{2}$$

The first term in (3) is the projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto the subspace spanned by $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ (the line through $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and the origin), and the second term is the projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto the subspace spanned by $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ . Thus (3) expresses $$\textbf{y}$$ as the sum of its projections onto the (orthogonal) axes determined by $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ . See Figure 4.

image.alt: A figure shows two vectors perpendicular to each other along with a point y and its projections on both vectors.

figure.caption: Figure 4 A vector decomposed into the sum of two projections

section.paragraph: Theorem 5 decomposes each $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ into the sum of $$p$$ projections onto one-dimensional subspaces that are mutually orthogonal.
section.heading: Decomposing a Force into Component Forces
section.paragraph: The decomposition in Figure 4 can occur in physics when some sort of force is applied to an object. Choosing an appropriate coordinate system allows the force to be represented by a vector $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ or $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . Often the problem involves some particular direction of interest, which is represented by another vector $$\mathbf{u}$$ . For instance, if the object is moving in a straight line when the force is applied, the vector $$\mathbf{u}$$ might point in the direction of movement, as in Figure 5. A key step in the problem is to decompose the force into a component in the direction of $$\mathbf{u}$$ and a component orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}$$ . The calculations would be analogous to those previously made in Example 3.

image.alt: A photo shows a car being towed by a tow truck with three vectors pointing from the front end car. The vector along a towing cable is represented as y. The horizontal vector is labeled u and the vertical vector is unnamed.

figure.caption: Figure 5

section.heading: Orthonormal Sets
section.paragraph: A set $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ is an orthonormal set if it is an orthogonal set of unit vectors. If $$W$$ is the subspace spanned by such a set, then $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ is an orthonormal basis for $$W$$ , since the set is automatically linearly independent, by Theorem 4.

The simplest example of an orthonormal set is the standard basis $$\left\{ \textbf{e}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \textbf{e}_{n} \right\}$$ for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Any nonempty subset of $$\left\{ \textbf{e}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \textbf{e}_{n} \right\}$$ is orthonormal, too. Here is a more complicated example.

example.paragraph: Show that $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ is an orthonormal basis of $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ , where

Thus $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal set. Also,

Thus $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ is an orthonormal set. Since the set is linearly independent, its three vectors form a basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . See Figure 6.

figure.caption: Figure 6

section.paragraph: When the vectors in an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors are normalized to have unit length, the new vectors will still be orthogonal, and hence the new set will be an orthonormal set. See Exercise 40. It is easy to check that the vectors in Figure 6 (Example ﻿﻿5) are simply the unit vectors in the directions of the vectors in Figure 1 (Example ﻿1).
Matrices whose columns form an orthonormal set are important in applications and in computer algorithms for matrix computations. Their main properties are given in Theorems 6 and 7.

note.title: Theorem ﻿6
note.heading: Theorem ﻿6
note.paragraph: An $$m \times n$$ matrix $$U$$ has orthonormal columns if and only if $$U^{T} U = I$$ .

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: To simplify notation, we suppose that $$U$$ has only three columns, each a vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ . The proof of the general case is essentially the same. Let $$U = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} \mathbf{u}_{1} & \mathbf{u}_{2} & \mathbf{u}_{3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and compute

$$U^{T} U = \left[\right. \mathbf{u}_{1}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{2}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{3}^{T} \left]\right. \left[\right. u_{1} & u_{2} & u_{3} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \mathbf{u}_{1}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{1} & \mathbf{u}_{1}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{2} & \mathbf{u}_{1}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{3} \mathbf{u}_{2}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{1} & \mathbf{u}_{2}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{2} & \mathbf{u}_{2}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{3} \mathbf{u}_{3}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{1} & \mathbf{u}_{3}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{2} & \mathbf{u}_{3}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{3} \left]\right.$$
The entries in the matrix at the right are inner products, using transpose notation. The columns of $$U$$ are orthogonal if and only if

$$\mathbf{u}_{1}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{2} = \mathbf{u}_{2}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{1} = 0 , \mathbf{u}_{1}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{3} = \mathbf{u}_{3}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{1} = 0 , \mathbf{u}_{2}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{3} = \mathbf{u}_{3}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{2} = 0$$
The columns of $$U$$ all have unit length if and only if
$$\mathbf{u}_{1}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{1} = 1 , \mathbf{u}_{2}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{2} = 1 , \mathbf{u}_{3}^{T} \mathbf{u}_{3} = 1$$
The theorem follows immediately from (4)–(6).

note.title: Theorem ﻿7
note.heading: Theorem ﻿7
note.paragraph: Let $$U$$ be an $$m \times n$$ matrix with orthonormal columns, and let $$\textbf{x}$$ and $$\textbf{y}$$ be in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Then

list.item: $$\parallel U \textbf{x} \parallel = \parallel \textbf{x} \parallel$$
$$\left(U \textbf{x}\right) \cdot \left(U \textbf{y}\right) = \textbf{x} \cdot \textbf{y}$$
$$\left( {U\textbf{x}} \right) \cdot \left( {U\textbf{y}} \right) = 0$$ if and only if $$\textbf{x} \cdot \textbf{y} = 0$$

section.paragraph: Properties (a) and (c) say that the linear mapping $$\textbf{x}\mapsto U\textbf{x}$$ preserves lengths and orthogonality. These properties are crucial for many computer algorithms. See Exercise 33 for the proof of Theorem 7.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Let $$U = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{cr} & \\ {1/\sqrt{2}} & {2/3} \\ {1/\sqrt{2}} & {- 2/3} \\ 0 & {1/3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\textbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} \sqrt{2} \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Notice that $$U$$ has orthonormal columns and

$$U^{T} U = \left[\right. 1 / \sqrt{2} & 1 / \sqrt{2} & 0 2 / 3 & - 2 / 3 & 1 / 3 \left]\right. \left[\right. 1 / \sqrt{2} & 2 / 3 1 / \sqrt{2} & - 2 / 3 0 & 1 / 3 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 1 & 0 0 & 1 \left]\right.$$
Verify that $$\text{∥} U\textbf{x} \text{∥} = \text{∥} \textbf{x} \text{∥}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: $$U \textbf{x} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 / \sqrt{2} & 2 / 3 \\ 1 / \sqrt{2} & - 2 / 3 \\ 0 & 1 / 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\sqrt{2} \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ - 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. \parallel U \textbf{x} \parallel & = & \sqrt{9 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{11} \parallel \textbf{x} \parallel & = & \sqrt{2 + 9} = \sqrt{11}$$

section.paragraph: Theorem 6 and 7 are particularly useful when applied to square matrices. An orthogonal matrix is a square invertible matrix $$U$$ such that $$U^{- 1} = U^{T}$$ . By Theorem 6, such a matrix has orthonormal columns.1 It is easy to see that any square matrix with orthonormal columns is an orthogonal matrix. Surprisingly, such a matrix must have orthonormal rows, too. See Exercises 35 and 36. Orthogonal matrices will appear frequently in Chapter 7.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: The matrix
$$U = \left[\right. 3 / \sqrt{11} & - 1 / \sqrt{6} & - 1 / \sqrt{66} 1 / \sqrt{11} & 2 / \sqrt{6} & - 4 / \sqrt{66} 1 / \sqrt{11} & 1 / \sqrt{6} & 7 / \sqrt{66} \left]\right.$$
is an orthogonal matrix because it is square and because its columns are orthonormal, by Example 5. Verify that the rows are orthonormal, too!

list.item: Let $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1/\sqrt{5}} \\ {2/\sqrt{5}} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {2/\sqrt{5}} \\ {1/\sqrt{5}} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Show that $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ is an orthonormal basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ .

Let $$\textbf{y}$$ and $$L$$ be as in Example 3 and Figure 3. Compute the orthogonal projection $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$L$$ using $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ instead of the $$\mathbf{u}$$ in Example 3.

Let $$U$$ and $$\textbf{x}$$ be as in Example 6, and let $$\textbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} {- 3\sqrt{2}} \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Verify that $$U\textbf{x} \cdot U\textbf{y} = \textbf{x} \cdot \textbf{y}$$ .
Let $$U$$ be an $$n \times n$$ matrix with orthonormal columns. Show that $$det$$ $$U = \pm 1$$ .

problem.paragraph: [T] Show that the columns of the matrix $$A$$ are orthogonal by making an appropriate matrix calculation. State the calculation you use.
[T] In parts (a)–(d), let $$U$$ be the matrix formed by normalizing each column of the matrix $$A$$ in Exercise 43.

list.item: Compute $$U^{T} U$$ and $$UU^{T}$$ . How do they differ?

Generate a random vector $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{8}$$ , and compute $$\textbf{p} = UU^{T}\textbf{y}$$ and $$\textbf{z} = \textbf{y} - \textbf{p}$$ . Explain why $$\textbf{p}$$ is in $$\text{Col} A$$ . Verify that $$\textbf{z}$$ is orthogonal to $$\textbf{p}$$ .
Verify that $$\textbf{z}$$ is orthogonal to each column of $$U$$ .

Notice that $$\textbf{y} = \textbf{p} + \textbf{z}$$ , with $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$\text{Col} A$$ . Explain why $$\textbf{z}$$ is in $${( \text{Col} A)}^{\bot}$$ . (The significance of this decomposition of $$\textbf{y}$$ will be explained in the next section.)

problem.paragraph: The vectors are orthogonal because $$\textbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2} = - 2 / 5 + 2 / 5 = 0$$

They are unit vectors because $$\parallel \textbf{u}_{1} \parallel^{2} = \left(- 1 / \sqrt{5}\right)^{2 } + \left(2 / \sqrt{5}\right)^{2} = 1 / 5 + 4 / 5 = 1 \parallel \textbf{u}_{2} \parallel^{2} = \left(2 / \sqrt{5}\right)^{2} + \left(1 / \sqrt{5}\right)^{2} = 4 / 5 + 1 / 5 = 1$$
In particular, the set $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ is linearly independent, and hence is a basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ since there are two vectors in the set.
When $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 7 \\ 6 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ ,

$$\widehat{\textbf{y}} = \frac{\mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u} = \frac{20}{5}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = 4\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$$ This is the same $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ found in Example 3. The orthogonal projection does not depend on the $$\mathbf{u}$$ chosen on the line. See Exercise 39.

$$U\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{cr} {1/\sqrt{2}} & {2/3} \\ {1/\sqrt{2}} & {- 2/3} \\ 0 & {1/3} \end{array} \right\rbrack\begin{bmatrix} {- 3\sqrt{2}} \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 7} \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ ﻿

Also, from Example 6, $$\textbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} \sqrt{2} \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$U\textbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Hence $$U \textbf{x} \cdot U \mathbf{y} = 3 + 7 + 2 = 12 ; \text{and} \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y} = - 6 + 18 = 12$$

Since $$U$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix with orthonormal columns, by Theorem 6, $$U^{T}U = I$$ . Taking the determinant of the left side of this equation, and applying Theorems 5 and 6 from Section 3.2 results in det $$U^{T}U = ({det} U^{T})({det} U) = ({det} U)({det} U) = ({det} U)^{2}$$ . Recall det $$I = 1$$ . Putting the two sides of the equation back together results in $$\left( \text{det} U \right)^{2} = 1$$ and hence det $$U = \pm 1$$ .

section.heading: 6.3 Orthogonal Projections
section.paragraph: The orthogonal projection of a point in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ onto a line through the origin has an important analogue in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Given a vector $$\textbf{y}$$ and a subspace $$W$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , there is a vector $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ in $$W$$ such that (1) $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is the unique vector in $$W$$ for which $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is orthogonal to $$W$$ , and (2) $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is the unique vector in $$W$$ closest to $$\textbf{y}$$ . See Figure 1. These two properties of $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ provide the key to finding least-squares solutions of linear systems.

image.alt: A figure shows a horizontal plane W with two vectors projecting from point 0 on the plane in the form of a right-angled triangle.

figure.caption: Watch Video

section.paragraph: To prepare for the first theorem, observe that whenever a vector $$\textbf{y}$$ is written as a linear combination of vectors $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{n}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the terms in the sum for $$\textbf{y}$$ can be grouped into two parts so that $$\textbf{y}$$ can be written as
$$\textbf{y} = \textbf{z}_{1} + \textbf{z}_{2}$$

where $$\textbf{z}_{1}$$ is a linear combination of some of the $$\mathbf{u}_{i}$$ and $$\textbf{z}_{2}$$ is a linear combination of the rest of the $$\mathbf{u}_{i}$$ . This idea is particularly useful when $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{n} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis. Recall from Section 6.1 that $$W^{\bot}$$ denotes the set of all vectors orthogonal to a subspace $$W$$ .

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Let $$\left\{ \textbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \textbf{u}_{5} \right\}$$ be an orthogonal basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{5}$$ and let
$$\textbf{y} = c_{1} \textbf{u}_{1} + \hdots + c_{5} \textbf{u}_{5}$$

Consider the subspace $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \textbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \textbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ , and write $$\textbf{y}$$ as the sum of a vector $$\textbf{z}_{1}$$ in $$W$$ and a vector $$\textbf{z}_{2}$$ in $$W^{\bot}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Write

$$\mathbf{y} = \underset{\mathbf{z}_{1}}{\underset{︸}{c_{1} \textbf{u}_{1} + c_{2} \textbf{u}_{2}}} + \underset{\mathbf{z}_{2}}{\underset{︸}{c_{3} \textbf{u}_{3} + c_{4} \textbf{u}_{4} + c_{5} \textbf{u}_{5}}}$$
where $$\textbf{z}_{1} = c_{1} \textbf{u}_{1} + c_{2} \textbf{u}_{2} \text{is in Span} \left{\right. \textbf{u}_{1} , \textbf{u}_{2} \left.\right}$$
and $$\textbf{z}_{2} = c_{3} \textbf{u}_{3} + c_{4} \textbf{u}_{4} + c_{5} \textbf{u}_{5} \text{is in Span} \left{\right. \textbf{u}_{3} , \textbf{u}_{4} , \textbf{u}_{5} \left.\right} .$$

To show that $$\textbf{z}_{2}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ , it suffices to show that $$\textbf{z}_{2}$$ is orthogonal to the vectors in the basis $$\left\{ \textbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \textbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ for $$W$$ . (See Section 6.1.) Using properties of the inner product, compute

$$\textbf{z}_{2} \cdot \textbf{u}_{1} & = & \left(\right. c_{3} \textbf{u}_{3} + c_{4} \textbf{u}_{4} + c_{5} \textbf{u}_{5} \left.\right) \cdot \textbf{u}_{1} & = & c_{3} \textbf{u}_{3} \cdot \textbf{u}_{1} + c_{4} \textbf{u}_{4} \cdot \textbf{u}_{1} + c_{5} \textbf{u}_{5} \cdot \textbf{u}_{1} & = & 0$$

because $$\textbf{u}_{1}$$ is orthogonal to $$\textbf{u}_{3}$$ , $$\textbf{u}_{4}$$ , and $$\textbf{u}_{5}$$ . A similar calculation shows that $$\textbf{z}_{2} \cdot \textbf{u}_{2} = 0$$ . Thus $$\textbf{z}_{2}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ .

section.paragraph: The next theorem shows that the decomposition $$\textbf{y} = \textbf{z}_{1} + \textbf{z}_{2}$$ in Example 1 can be computed without having an orthogonal basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . It is enough to have an orthogonal basis only for $$W$$ .

note.title: Theorem 8
note.heading: Theorem 8
The Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $$W$$ be a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Then each $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ can be written uniquely in the form
$$\textbf{y} = \hat{\textbf{y}} + \textbf{z}$$

where $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is in $$W$$ and $$\textbf{z}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ . In fact, if $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ is any orthogonal basis of $$W$$ , then

$$\hat{\textbf{y}} = \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}}{\mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \hdots + \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{p}}{\mathbf{u}_{p} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{p}} \mathbf{u}_{p}$$
and $$\textbf{z} = \textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ .

section.paragraph: The vector $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ in (2) is called the orthogonal projection of y onto $$W$$ and often is written as $$\text{proj} _{W}{\textbf{y}}$$ . See Figure 2. When $$W$$ is a one-dimensional subspace, the formula for $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ matches the formula given in Section 6.2.
section.heading: Figure 2
section.paragraph: The orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ ﻿onto $$W$$

image.alt: A figure shows a horizontal plane W with three vectors projecting from point 0 on the plane.

figure.caption: Figure 1

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: Let $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ be any orthogonal basis for $$W$$ , and define $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ by (2).1 Then $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is in $$W$$ because $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is a linear combination of the basis $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{p}$$ . Let $$\textbf{z} = \textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ . Since $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ is orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{p}$$ , it follows from ( $$2$$ ) that

$$\left(\textbf{z} \cdot \mathbf{u}\right)_{1} = ( \textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} ) \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} & = & \left(\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}\right)_{1} - \left(\frac{\textbf{y}\cdot\textbf{u}_{1}}{\textbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}}\right) \mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} - 0 - \hdots - 0 & = & \left(\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}\right)_{1} - \left(\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}\right)_{1} = 0$$

Thus $$\textbf{z}$$ is orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ . Similarly, $$\textbf{z}$$ is orthogonal to each $$\mathbf{u}_{j}$$ in the basis for $$W$$ . Hence $$\textbf{z}$$ is orthogonal to every vector in $$W$$ . That is, $$\textbf{z}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ .

To show that the decomposition in (1) is unique, suppose $$\textbf{y}$$ can also be written as $$\textbf{y} = {\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1} + \textbf{z}_{1}$$ , with $${\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1}$$ in $$W$$ and $$\textbf{z}_{1}$$ in $$W^{\bot}$$ . Then $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} + \textbf{z} = {\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1} + \textbf{z}_{1}$$ (since both sides equal $$\textbf{y}$$ ), and so
$$\hat{\textbf{y}} - \left(\hat{\textbf{y}}\right)_{1} = \textbf{z}_{1} - \textbf{z}$$

This equality shows that the vector $$\mathbf{v} = \widehat{\textbf{y}} - {\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1}$$ is in $$W$$ and in $$W^{\bot}$$ (because $$\textbf{z}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{z}$$ are both in $$W^{\bot}$$ , and $$W^{\bot}$$ is a subspace). Hence $$\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$$ , which shows that $$\mathbf{v} = \textbf{0}$$ . This proves that $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} = {\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1}$$ and also $$\textbf{z}_{1} = \textbf{z}$$ .
The uniqueness of the decomposition (1) shows that the orthogonal projection $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ depends only on $$W$$ and not on the particular basis used in (2).

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 5 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Observe that $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ . Write $$\textbf{y}$$ as the sum of a vector in $$W$$ and a vector orthogonal to $$W$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$W$$ is

$$\hat{\textbf{y}} & = & \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}}{\mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \frac{\left(\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}\right)_{2}}{\mathbf{u}_{2} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2}} \mathbf{u}_{2} & = & \frac{9}{30} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 5 \\ - 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. + \frac{3}{6} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \frac{9}{30} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 5 \\ - 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. + \frac{15}{30} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 2 / 5 \\ 2 \\ 1 / 5\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$
Also
$$\textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} = \left[\right. 1 2 3 \left]\right. - \left[\right. - 2 / 5 2 1 / 5 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 7 / 5 0 14 / 5 \left]\right.$$

Theorem 8 ensures that $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ . To check the calculations, however, it is a good idea to verify that $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is orthogonal to both $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ and hence to all of $$W$$ . The desired decomposition of $$\textbf{y}$$ is
$$\textbf{y} = \left[\right. 1 2 3 \left]\right. = \left[\right. - 2 / 5 2 1 / 5 \left]\right. + \left[\right. 7 / 5 0 14 / 5 \left]\right.$$

section.heading: A Geometric Interpretation of the Orthogonal Projection
section.paragraph: When $$W$$ is a one-dimensional subspace, the formula (2) for $$\text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ contains just one term. Thus, when $$\dim W > 1$$ , each term in (2) is itself an orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto a one-dimensional subspace spanned by one of the $$\mathbf{u}’s$$ in the basis for $$W$$ . Figure 3 illustrates this when $$W$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ spanned by $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ . Here $${\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1}$$ and $${\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{2}$$ denote the projections of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto the lines spanned by $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ , respectively. The orthogonal projection $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$W$$ is the sum of the projections of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto one-dimensional subspaces that are orthogonal to each other. The vector $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ in Figure 3 corresponds to the vector $$\textbf{y}$$ in Figure 4 of Section 6.2, because now it is $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ that is in $$W$$ .

image.alt: A graph shows the orthogonal projection of y with mutually orthogonal subspaces on a three-dimensional axis.

figure.caption: Figure 3 The orthogonal projection of y ﻿is the sum of its projections onto one-dimensional subspaces that are mutually orthogonal

section.heading: Properties of Orthogonal Projections
section.paragraph: If $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$W$$ and if $$\textbf{y}$$ happens to be in $$W$$ , then the formula for $$\text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ is exactly the same as the representation of $$\textbf{y}$$ given in Theorem 5 in Section 6.2. In this case, $$\text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y} = \textbf{y}$$ .
This fact also follows from the next theorem.

note.title: Theorem 9
note.heading: Theorem 9
T﻿he Best Approximation Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $$W$$ be a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , let $$\textbf{y}$$ be any vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , and let $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ be the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$W$$ . Then $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is the closest point in $$W$$ to $$\textbf{y}$$ , in the sense that
$$\parallel \textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} \parallel < \parallel \textbf{y} - \mathbf{v} \parallel$$
for all $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$W$$ distinct from $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ .

section.paragraph: The vector $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ in Theorem 9 is called the best approximation to $$\mathbf{y}$$ by elements of $$W$$ . Later sections in the text will examine problems where a given $$\textbf{y}$$ must be replaced, or approximated, by a vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ in some fixed subspace $$W$$ . The distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to $$\mathbf{v}$$ , given by $$\parallel \textbf{y} - \mathbf{v} \parallel$$ , can be regarded as the “error” of using $$\mathbf{v}$$ in place of $$\textbf{y}$$ . Theorem 9 says that this error is minimized when $$\mathbf{v} = \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ .

Inequality (3) leads to a new proof that $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ does not depend on the particular orthogonal basis used to compute it. If a different orthogonal basis for $$W$$ was used to construct an orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ , then this projection would also be the closest point in $$W$$ to $$\textbf{y}$$ , namely $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ .
section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Take $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$W$$ distinct from $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ . See Figure 4. Then $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} - \mathbf{v}$$ is in $$W$$ . By the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem, $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is orthogonal to $$W$$ . In particular, $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is orthogonal to $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} - \mathbf{v}$$ (which is in $$W$$ ). Since
$$\textbf{y} - \mathbf{v} = \left(\right. \textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} \left.\right) + \left(\right. \hat{\textbf{y}} - \mathbf{v} \left.\right)$$
the Pythagorean Theorem gives
$$\parallel \textbf{y} - \mathbf{v} \parallel^{2} = \parallel \textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} \parallel^{2} + \parallel \hat{\textbf{y}} - \mathbf{v} \parallel^{2}$$

(See the right triangle outlined in teal in Figure 4. The length of each side is labeled.) Now $$\text{∥} \widehat{\textbf{y}} - \mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2} > 0$$ because $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} - \mathbf{v} \neq \textbf{0}$$ , and so inequality (3) follows immediately.

image.alt: A figure shows the orthogonal projection of y onto a horizontal plane W with two right-angled triangles with the same altitude.

figure.caption: Figure 4 The orthogonal projection of y onto ﻿ W is the closest point in ﻿ W ﻿to y

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 5 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ , as in Example 2, then the closest point in $$W$$ to $$\textbf{y}$$ is

$$\hat{\textbf{y}} = \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}}{\mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2}}{\mathbf{u}_{2} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2}} \mathbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. - 2 / 5 2 1 / 5 \left]\right.$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: The distance from a point $$\textbf{y}$$ in $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ to a subspace $$W$$ is defined as the distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to the nearest point in $$W$$ . Find the distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ , where
$$\textbf{y} = \left[\right. - 1 - 5 10 \left]\right. , \mathbf{u}_{1} = \left[\right. 5 - 2 1 \left]\right. , \mathbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. 1 2 - 1 \left]\right.$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: By the Best Approximation Theorem, the distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to $$W$$ is $$\parallel \textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}} \parallel$$ , where $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} = \text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ . Since $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$W$$ ,

$$\hat{\textbf{y}} & = & \frac{15}{30} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \frac{- 21}{6} \mathbf{u}_{2} = \frac{1}{2} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5 \\ - 2 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. - \frac{7}{2} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 2 \\ - 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ - 8 \\ 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. \textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ - 5 \\ 10\end{matrix} \left]\right. - \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ - 8 \\ 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{matrix} \left]\right. \parallel \textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} \parallel^{2} & = & 3^{2} + 6^{2} = 45$$
The distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to $$W$$ is $$\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}$$ .

section.paragraph: The final theorem in this section shows how formula (2) for $$\text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ is simplified when the basis for $$W$$ is an orthonormal set.

note.title: Theorem ﻿10
note.heading: Theorem ﻿10
note.paragraph: If $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ is an orthonormal basis for a subspace $$W$$ of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then

$$\text{proj} _{W } \textbf{y} = ( \textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} ) \mathbf{u}_{1} + ( \textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2} ) \mathbf{u}_{2} + \hdots + ( \textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{p} ) \mathbf{u}_{p}$$
If $$U = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrrr} \mathbf{u}_{1} & \mathbf{u}_{2} & \cdots & \mathbf{u}_{p} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , then
$$\text{proj} _{W} \textbf{y} = U U^{T} \textbf{y} \text{for all} \textbf{y} \text{in} \mathbb{R}^{n}$$

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: Formula (4) follows immediately from (2) in Theorem 8. Also, (4) shows that $$\text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ is a linear combination of the columns of $$U$$ using the weights $$\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}$$ , $$\mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{p}$$ . The weights can be written as $$\mathbf{u}_{1}^{T}\textbf{y}$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2}^{T}\textbf{y}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{p}^{T}\textbf{y}$$ , showing that they are the entries in $$U^{T}\textbf{y}$$ and justifying (5).
Suppose $$U$$ is an $$n \times p$$ matrix with orthonormal columns, and let $$W$$ be the column space of $$U$$ . Then

$$U^{T} U \textbf{x} & = & I_{p} \textbf{x} = \textbf{x} & \text{for all} \textbf{x} \text{in} \mathbb{R}^{p} & \text{Theorem} 6 U U^{T} \textbf{y} & = & \text{proj} _{W} \textbf{y} & \text{for all} \textbf{y} \text{in} \mathbb{R}^{n} & \text{Theorem} 10$$

If $$U$$ is an $$n \times n$$ (square) matrix with orthonormal columns, then $$U$$ is an orthogonal matrix, the column space $$W$$ is all of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , and $$UU^{T}\textbf{y} = I\textbf{y} = \textbf{y}$$ for all $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

Although formula (4) is important for theoretical purposes, in practice it usually involves calculations with square roots of numbers (in the entries of the $$\mathbf{u}_{i}$$ ). Formula (2) is recommended for hand calculations.

Example 9 of Section 2.1 illustrates how matrix multiplication and transposition are used to detect a specified pattern illustrated using blue and white squares. Now that we have more experience working with bases for $$W$$ and $$W^{\bot}$$ , we are ready to discuss how to set up the matrix $$M$$ in Figure 6. Let $$\textbf{w}$$ be the vector generated from a pattern of blue and white squares by turning each blue square into a $$1$$ and each white square into a $$0$$ , and then lining up each column below the column before it. See Figure 5.

image.alt: A figure shows creation of a vector from colored squares.

figure.caption: Figure 5 Creating a vector from colored squares

section.paragraph: Let $$W = \text{span} \left\{ \textbf{w} \right\}$$ . Choose a basis $$\left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n - 1} \right\}$$ for $$W^{\bot}$$ . Create the matrix $$B = \begin{bmatrix} {\textbf{v}_{1}}^{T} \\ {\textbf{v}_{2}}^{T} \\ \vdots \\ {\textbf{v}_{n - 1}}^{T} \end{bmatrix}$$ . Notice $$B\textbf{u} = \textbf{0}$$ if and only if $$\textbf{u}$$ is orthogonal to a set of basis vectors for $$W^{\bot}$$ , which happens if and only if $$\textbf{u}$$ is in $$W$$ . Set $$M = B^{T}B$$ . Then $$\textbf{u}^{T}M\textbf{u} = \textbf{u}^{T}B^{T}B\textbf{u} = {(B\textbf{u})}^{T}B\textbf{u}$$ . By Theorem 1, $${(B\textbf{u})}^{T}B\textbf{u} = 0$$ if and only if $$B\textbf{u} = 0$$ , and hence $$\textbf{u}^{T}M\textbf{u} = 0$$ if and only if $$\textbf{u} \in W$$ . But there are only two vectors in $$W$$ consisting of zeros and ones: $$1\textbf{w} = \textbf{w}$$ and $$0\textbf{w} = \textbf{0}$$ . Thus we can conclude that if $$\textbf{u}^{T}M\textbf{u} = 0$$ , but $$\textbf{u}^{T}\textbf{u} \neq 0$$ , then $$\textbf{u} = \textbf{w}$$ . See Figure 6.

list.item: Let $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 7} \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \\ {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 9} \\ 1 \\ 6 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ . Use the fact that $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ are orthogonal to compute $$\text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ .

Let $$W$$ be a subspace of $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Let $$\textbf{x}$$ and $$\textbf{y}$$ be vectors in $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ and let $$\textbf{z} = \textbf{x} + \textbf{y}$$ . If $$\mathbf{u}$$ is the projection of $$\textbf{x}$$ onto $$W$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ is the projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$W$$ , show that $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$$ is the projection of $$\textbf{z}$$ onto $$W$$ .

section.paragraph: 1 We may assume that $$W$$ is not the zero subspace, for otherwise $$W^{\bot} = \mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and (1) is simply $$\textbf{y} = \textbf{0} + \textbf{y}$$ . The next section will show that any nonzero subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ has an orthogonal basis.

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 1 and 2, you may assume that $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{4} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ .

problem.paragraph: $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 1 \\ {- 4} \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 5 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{3} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ {- 4} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{4} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ {- 3} \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\textbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 10 \\ {- 8} \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Write $$\textbf{x}$$ as the sum of two vectors, one in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{3} \right\}$$ and the other in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{4} \right\}$$ .

$$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 1 \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{3} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \\ {- 2} \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{4} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 4 \\ 5 \\ {- 2} \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Write $$\mathbf{v}$$ as the sum of two vectors, one in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \right\}$$ and the other in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{3} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{4} \right\}$$ .

problem.paragraph: $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 4 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. - 1 1 0 \left]\right.$$
