section.heading: 6.8 Applications of Inner Product Spaces
section.paragraph: The examples in this section suggest how the inner product spaces defined in Section 6.7 arise in practical problems. Like in Section 6.6, important components of machine learning are analyzed.
section.heading: Weighted Least-Squares
section.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{y}$$ be a vector of $$n$$ observations, $$y_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$y_{n}$$ , and suppose we wish to approximate $$\textbf{y}$$ by a vector $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ that belongs to some specified subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . (In Section 6.5, $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ was written as $$A\textbf{x}$$ so that $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ was in the column space of $$A$$ .) Denote the entries in $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ by $${\widehat{y}}_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $${\widehat{y}}_{n}$$ . Then the sum of the squares for error, or $$\text{SS(E)}$$ , in approximating $$\textbf{y}$$ by $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is
$$\text{SS} ( \text{E} ) = \left(\right. y_{1} - \left(\hat{y}\right)_{1} \left.\right)^{2} + \hdots + \left(\right. y_{n} - \left(\hat{y}\right)_{n} \left.\right)^{2}$$
This is simply $$\parallel \textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}} \parallel^{2}$$ , using the standard length in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

Now suppose the measurements that produced the entries in $$\textbf{y}$$ are not equally reliable. The entries in $$\textbf{y}$$ might be computed from various samples of measurements, with unequal sample sizes. Then it becomes appropriate to weight the squared errors in (1) in such a way that more importance is assigned to the more reliable measurements.1 If the weights are denoted by $$w_{1}^{2}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$w_{n}^{2}$$ , then the weighted sum of the squares for error is
$$\text{Weighted SS} ( \text{E} ) = w_{1}^{2} \left(\right. y_{1} - \left(\hat{y}\right)_{1} \left.\right)^{2} + \hdots + w_{n}^{2} \left(\right. y_{n} - \left(\hat{y}\right)_{n} \left.\right)^{2}$$
This is the square of the length of $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ , where the length is derived from an inner product analogous to that in Example 1 in Section 6.7, namely
$$\langle \textbf{x} , \textbf{y} \rangle = w_{1}^{2} x_{1} y_{1} + \hdots + w_{n}^{2} x_{n} y_{n}$$

It is sometimes convenient to transform a weighted least-squares problem into an equivalent ordinary least-squares problem. Let $$W$$ be the diagonal matrix with (positive) $$w_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$w_{n}$$ on its diagonal, so that

$$W \textbf{y} = \left[\right. w_{1} & 0 & \hdots & 0 0 & w_{2} & & \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots 0 & & \hdots & w_{n} \left]\right. \left[\right. y_{1} y_{2} \vdots y_{n} \left]\right. = \left[\right. w_{1} y_{1} w_{2} y_{2} \vdots w_{n} y_{n} \left]\right.$$
with a similar expression for $$W\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ . Observe that the $$j$$ th term in (2) can be written as
$$w_{j}^{2} \left(\right. y_{j} - \left(\hat{y}\right)_{j} \left.\right)^{2} = \left(\right. w_{j} y_{j} - w_{j} \left(\hat{y}\right)_{j} \left.\right)^{2}$$

It follows that the weighted $$\text{SS(E)}$$ in (2) is the square of the ordinary length in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ of $$W\textbf{y} - W\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ , which we write as $$\parallel W\textbf{y} - W\widehat{\textbf{y}} \parallel^{2}$$ .

Now suppose the approximating vector $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is to be constructed from the columns of a matrix $$A$$ . Then we seek an $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ that makes $$A\widehat{\textbf{x}} = \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ as close to $$\textbf{y}$$ as possible. However, the measure of closeness is the weighted error,
$$\parallel W \textbf{y} - W \hat{\textbf{y}} \parallel^{2} = \parallel W \textbf{y} - W A \hat{\textbf{x}} \parallel^{2}$$
Thus $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ is the (ordinary) least-squares solution of the equation
$$W A \textbf{x} = W \textbf{y}$$
The normal equation for the least-squares solution is
$$\boxed{\left(\right. W A \left.\right)^{T} W A \textbf{x} = \left(\right. W A \left.\right)^{T} W \textbf{y}}$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Find the least-squares line $$y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x$$ that best fits the data $$\left( - 2 \text{,} 3 \right)$$ , $$\left( - 1 \text{,} 5 \right)$$ , $$\left( 0 \text{,} 5 \right)$$ , $$\left( 1 \text{,} 4 \right)$$ , and $$\left( 2 \text{,} 3 \right)$$ . Suppose the errors in measuring the $$y \text{-values}$$ of the last two data points are greater than for the other points. Weight these data half as much as the rest of the data.

$$X = \left[\right. 1 & - 2 1 & - 1 1 & 0 1 & 1 1 & 2 \left]\right. , \mathbf{\mathit{\beta}} = \left[\right. \beta_{0} \beta_{1} \left]\right. , \textbf{y} = \left[\right. 3 5 5 4 3 \left]\right.$$
For a weighting matrix, choose $$W$$ with diagonal entries $$2$$ , $$2$$ , $$2$$ , $$1$$ , and $$1$$ . Left-multiplication by $$W$$ scales the rows of $$X$$ and $$\textbf{y}$$ :
$$W X = \left[\right. 2 & - 4 2 & - 2 2 & 0 1 & 1 1 & 2 \left]\right. , W \textbf{y} = \left[\right. 6 10 10 4 3 \left]\right.$$
For the normal equation, compute
$$\left(( W X )\right)^{T} = \left[\right. 14 & - 9 - 9 & 25 \left]\right. \text{and} ( W X )^{T} W \textbf{y} = \left[\right. 59 - 34 \left]\right.$$
and solve
$$\left[\right. 14 & - 9 - 9 & 25 \left]\right. \left[\right. \beta_{0} \beta_{1} \left]\right. = \left[\right. 59 - 34 \left]\right.$$
The solution of the normal equation is (to two significant digits) $$\beta_{0} = 4.3$$ and $$\beta_{1} = .20$$ . The desired line is

section.heading: Trend Analysis of Data
section.paragraph: Let $$f$$ represent an unknown function whose values are known (perhaps only approximately) at $$t_{0}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$t_{n}$$ . If there is a “linear trend” in the data $$f\left( t_{0} \right)$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$f\left( t_{n} \right)$$ , then we might expect to approximate the values of $$f$$ by a function of the form $$\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}t$$ . If there is a “quadratic trend” to the data, then we would try a function of the form $$\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}t + \beta_{2}t^{2}$$ . This was discussed in Section 6.6, from a different point of view.

In some statistical problems, it is important to be able to separate the linear trend from the quadratic trend (and possibly cubic or higher-order trends). For instance, suppose engineers are analyzing the performance of a new car, and $$f(t)$$ represents the distance between the car at time $$t$$ and some reference point. If the car is traveling at constant velocity, then the graph of $$f(t)$$ should be a straight line whose slope is the car’s velocity. If the gas pedal is suddenly pressed to the floor, the graph of $$f(t)$$ will change to include a quadratic term and possibly a cubic term (due to the acceleration). To analyze the ability of the car to pass another car, for example, engineers may want to separate the quadratic and cubic components from the linear term.

If the function is approximated by a curve of the form $$y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}t + \beta_{2}t^{2}$$ , the coefficient $$\beta_{2}$$ may not give the desired information about the quadratic trend in the data, because it may not be “independent” in a statistical sense from the other $$\beta_{i}$$ . To make what is known as a trend analysis of the data, we introduce an inner product on the space $$\text{ℙ} _{n}$$ analogous to that given in Example 2 in Section 6.7. For $$p$$ , $$q$$ in $$\text{ℙ} _{n}$$ , define
$$\langle p , q \rangle = p \left(\right. t_{0} \left.\right) q \left(\right. t_{0} \left.\right) + \hdots + p \left(\right. t_{n} \left.\right) q \left(\right. t_{n} \left.\right)$$

In practice, statisticians seldom need to consider trends in data of degree higher than cubic or quartic. So let $$p_{0}$$ , $$p_{1}$$ , $$p_{2}$$ , $$p_{3}$$ denote an orthogonal basis of the subspace $$\text{ℙ} _{3}$$ of $$\text{ℙ} _{n}$$ , obtained by applying the Gram–Schmidt process to the polynomials $$1$$ , $$t$$ , $$t^{2}$$ , and $$t^{3}$$ . There is a polynomial $$g$$ in $$\text{ℙ} _{n}$$ whose values at $$t_{0}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$t_{n}$$ coincide with those of the unknown function $$f$$ . Let $$\widehat{g}$$ be the orthogonal projection (with respect to the given inner product) of $$g$$ onto $$\text{ℙ} _{3}$$ , say,

Then $$\widehat{g}$$ is called a cubic trend function, and $$c_{0}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$c_{3}$$ are the trend coefficients of the data. The coefficient $$c_{1}$$ measures the linear trend, $$c_{2}$$ the quadratic trend, and $$c_{3}$$ the cubic trend. It turns out that if the data have certain properties, these coefficients are statistically independent.

Since $$p_{0}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$p_{3}$$ are orthogonal, the trend coefficients may be computed one at a time, independently of one another. (Recall that $$c_{i} = \left\langle g \text{,} p_{i} \right\rangle/\left\langle p_{i} \text{,} p_{i} \right\rangle$$ .) We can ignore $$p_{3}$$ and $$c_{3}$$ if we want only the quadratic trend. And if, for example, we needed to determine the quartic trend, we would have to find (via Gram–Schmidt) only a polynomial $$p_{4}$$ in $$\text{ℙ} _{4}$$ that is orthogonal to $$\text{ℙ} _{3}$$ and compute $$\left\langle g \text{,} p_{4} \right\rangle/\left\langle p_{4} \text{,} p_{4} \right\rangle$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: The simplest and most common use of trend analysis occurs when the points $$t_{0}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$t_{n}$$ can be adjusted so that they are evenly spaced and sum to zero. Fit a quadratic trend function to the data $$\left( - 2 \text{,} 3 \right)$$ , $$\left( - 1 \text{,} 5 \right)$$ , $$\left( 0 \text{,} 5 \right)$$ , $$\left( 1 \text{,} 4 \right)$$ , and $$\left( 2 \text{,} 3 \right)$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The $$t \text{-coordinates}$$ are suitably scaled to use the orthogonal polynomials found in Example 5 of Section 6.7:

$$\text{Polynomial} & p_{0} & p_{1} & p_{2} & \text{Data} : g \text{Vector} \text{of} \text{values} & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 2 \\ - 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ - 1 \\ - 2 \\ - 1 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 5 \\ 5 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

The calculations involve only these vectors, not the specific formulas for the orthogonal polynomials. The best approximation to the data by polynomials in $$\text{ℙ} _{2}$$ is the orthogonal projection given by

$$\hat{p} & = & \frac{\langle g , p_{0} \rangle}{\langle p_{0} , p_{0} \rangle} p_{0} + \frac{\langle g , p_{1} \rangle}{\langle p_{1} , p_{1} \rangle} p_{1} + \frac{\langle g , p_{2} \rangle}{\langle p_{2} , p_{2} \rangle} p_{2} & = & \frac{20}{5} p_{0} - \frac{1}{10} p_{1} - \frac{7}{14} p_{2}$$
and
Since the coefficient of $$p_{2}$$ is not extremely small, it would be reasonable to conclude that the trend is at least quadratic. This is confirmed by the graph in Figure 2.

section.heading: Fourier Series (Calculus required)
section.paragraph: Continuous functions are often approximated by linear combinations of sine and cosine functions. For instance, a continuous function might represent a sound wave, an electric signal of some type, or the movement of a vibrating mechanical system.

For simplicity, we consider functions on $$0 \leq t \leq 2\pi$$ . It turns out that any function in $$C\left\lbrack 0 \text{,} 2\pi \right\rbrack$$ can be approximated as closely as desired by a function of the form
$$\frac{a_{0}}{2} + a_{1} \cos t + \hdots + a_{n} \cos n t + b_{1} \sin t + \hdots + b_{n} \sin n t$$

for a sufficiently large value of $$n$$ . The function (4) is called a trigonometric polynomial. If $$a_{n}$$ and $$b_{n}$$ are not both zero, the polynomial is said to be of order $$\mathbf{n}$$ . The connection between trigonometric polynomials and other functions in $$C\left\lbrack 0 \text{,} 2\pi \right\rbrack$$ depends on the fact that for any $$n \geq 1$$ , the set
$$\left{\right. 1 , \cos t , \cos 2 t , \ldots , \cos n t , \sin t , \sin 2 t , \ldots , \sin n t \left.\right}$$
is orthogonal with respect to the inner product
$$\langle f , g \rangle = \int_{0}^{2 \pi} f ( t ) g ( t ) d t$$
This orthogonality is verified as in the following example and in Exercises 5 and 6.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Let $$C\lbrack 0 \text{,} 2\pi\rbrack$$ have the inner product (6), and let $$m$$ and $$n$$ be unequal positive integers. Show that $$\cos mt$$ and $$\cos nt$$ are orthogonal.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Use a trigonometric identity. When $$m \neq n$$ ,

$$\langle \cos m t ,\cos n t \rangle & = & \int_{0}^{2 \pi} \cos m t \cos n t d t & = & \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} [\cos \left(\right. m t + n t \left.\right) + \cos \left(\right. m t - n t ) ] d t & = & \left(\frac{1}{2} \left[\right. \frac{sin \left(\right. m t + n t \left.\right)}{m + n} + \frac{sin \left(\right. m t - n t \left.\right)}{m - n} \left]\right. \left|\right.\right)_{0}^{2 \pi} = 0$$

section.paragraph: Let $$W$$ be the subspace of $$C\lbrack 0 \text{,} 2\pi\rbrack$$ spanned by the functions in (5). Given $$f$$ in $$C\lbrack 0 \text{,} 2\pi\rbrack$$ , the best approximation to $$f$$ by functions in $$W$$ is called the $$n$$ th-order Fourier approximation to $$f$$ on $$\lbrack 0 \text{,} 2\pi\rbrack$$ . Since the functions in (5) are orthogonal, the best approximation is given by the orthogonal projection onto $$W$$ . In this case, the coefficients $$a_{k}$$ and $$b_{k}$$ in (4) are called the Fourier coefficients of $$f$$ . The standard formula for an orthogonal projection shows that
$$a_{k} = \frac{\langle f , \cos k t \rangle}{\langle \cos k t , \cos k t \rangle} , b_{k} = \frac{\langle f , \sin k t \rangle}{\langle \sin k t , \sin k t \rangle} , k \geq 1$$
Exercise 7 asks you to show that $$\left\langle \text{cos} kt \text{,} \text{cos} kt \right\rangle = \pi$$ and $$\left\langle \text{sin} kt \text{,} \text{sin} kt \right\rangle = \pi$$ . Thus
$$a_{k} = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} f ( t )\cos k t d t , b_{k} = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} f ( t )\sin k t d t$$
The coefficient of the (constant) function $$1$$ in the orthogonal projection is

$$\frac{\langle f , 1 \rangle}{\langle 1 , 1 \rangle} = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} f ( t ) \cdot 1 d t = \frac{1}{2} \left[\right. \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} f ( t )\cos ( 0 \cdot t ) d t \left]\right. = \frac{a_{0}}{2}$$
where $$a_{0}$$ is defined by (7) for $$k = 0$$ . This explains why the constant term in (4) is written as $$a_{0}/2$$ .

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the $$n$$ th-order Fourier approximation to the function $$f(t) = t$$ on the interval $$\lbrack 0 \text{,} 2\pi\rbrack$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Compute
$$\frac{a_{0}}{2} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} t d t = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \left[\right. \frac{1}{2} t^{2} \left|\right._{0}^{2 \pi} \left]\right. = \pi$$
and for $$k > 0$$ , using integration by parts,

$$a_{k} & = & \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} t \cos k t d t = \frac{1}{\pi} \left(\left[\right. \frac{1}{k^{2}} \cos k t + \frac{t}{k} \sin k t \left]\right.\right)_{0}^{2 \pi} = 0 b_{k} & = & \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} t \sin k t d t = \frac{1}{\pi} \left(\left[\right. \frac{1}{k^{2}} \sin k t - \frac{t}{k} \cos k t \left]\right.\right)_{0}^{2 \pi} = - \frac{2}{k}$$
Thus the $$n$$ th-order Fourier approximation of $$f(t) = t$$ is
$$\pi - 2 \sin t - \sin 2 t - \frac{2}{3} \sin 3 t - \hdots - \frac{2}{n} \sin n t$$
Figure 3 shows the third- and fourth-order Fourier approximations of $$f$$ .

image.alt: A graph shows third order Fourier approximation of the function f of t equals t.

figure.caption: Figure 3﻿ ﻿Fourier approximations of the function ﻿﻿ f(t)=t

image.alt: A graph shows fourth order Fourier approximation of the function f of t equals t.

section.paragraph: The norm of the difference between $$f$$ and a Fourier approximation is called the mean square error in the approximation. (The term mean refers to the fact that the norm is determined by an integral.) It can be shown that the mean square error approaches zero as the order of the Fourier approximation increases. For this reason, it is common to write
$$f ( t ) = \frac{a_{0}}{2} + \sum_{m = 1}^{\infty} ( a_{m} \cos m t + b_{m} \sin m t )$$

This expression for $$f(t)$$ is called the Fourier series for $$f$$ on $$\lbrack 0,2\pi\rbrack$$ . The term $$a_{m}\cos mt$$ , for example, is the projection of $$f$$ onto the one-dimensional subspace spanned by $$\cos mt$$ .

problem.paragraph: Compute $$\langle q_{1} , q_{2} \rangle = \int_{- 2}^{2} 1 \cdot t d t = \frac{1}{2} t^{2} \left|\right._{- 2}^{ 2} = 0 \langle q_{1} , q_{2} \rangle = \int_{- 2}^{2} 1 \cdot ( 3 t^{2} - 4 ) t d t = ( t^{3} - 4 t ) \left|\right._{- 2}^{ 2} = 0 \langle q_{1} , q_{2} \rangle = \int_{- 2}^{2} t \cdot ( 3 t^{2} - 4 ) t d t = \left(\right. \frac{3}{4} t^{4} - 2 t^{2} \left.\right) \left|\right._{- 2}^{ 2} = 0$$

The third-order Fourier approximation to $$f$$ is the best approximation in $$C\lbrack 0,2\pi\rbrack$$ to $$f$$ by functions (vectors) in the subspace spanned by $$1$$ , $$\cos t$$ , $$\cos 2t$$ , $$\cos 3t$$ , $$\sin t$$ , $$\sin 2t$$ , and $$\sin 3t$$ . But $$f$$ is obviously in this subspace, so $$f$$ is its own best approximation: $$f \left(t\right) = 3 - 2 sin t + 5 sin 2 t - 6 cos 2 t$$

For the first-order approximation, the closest function to $$f$$ in the subspace $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ 1,\cos t,\sin t \right\}$$ is $$3 - 2\sin t$$ . The other two terms in the formula for $$f(t)$$ are orthogonal to the functions in $$W$$ , so they contribute nothing to the integrals that give the Fourier coefficients for a first-order approximation.

section.paragraph: The statements in Exercises 1–19 refer to vectors in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ (or $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ ) with the standard inner product. Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

list.item: (T/F) The length of every vector is a positive number.
(T/F) A vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ and its negative, $$- \mathbf{v}$$ , have equal lengths.
(T/F) The distance between $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ is $$\parallel \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \parallel$$ .
(T/F) If $$r$$ is any scalar, then $$\text{∥} r\mathbf{v} \text{∥} = r \text{∥} \textbf{v} \text{∥}$$ .
(T/F) If two vectors are orthogonal, they are linearly independent.
(T/F) If $$\textbf{x}$$ is orthogonal to both $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ , then $$\textbf{x}$$ must be orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$$ .
(T/F) If $$\text{∥} \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2} = \text{∥} \textbf{u} \text{∥} ^{2} + \text{∥} \textbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2}$$ , then $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are orthogonal.
(T/F) If $$\text{∥} \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2} = \text{∥} \textbf{u} \text{∥} ^{2} + \text{∥} \textbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2}$$ , then $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are orthogonal.
(T/F) The orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$\mathbf{u}$$ is a scalar multiple of $$\textbf{y}$$ .
(T/F) If a vector $$\textbf{y}$$ coincides with its orthogonal projection onto a subspace $$W$$ , then $$\textbf{y}$$ is in $$W$$ .
(T/F) The set of all vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ orthogonal to one fixed vector is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .
(T/F) If $$W$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , then $$W$$ and $$W^{\bot}$$ have no vectors in common.

(T/F) If $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal set and if $$c_{1}$$ , $$c_{2}$$ , and $$c_{3}$$ are scalars, then $$\left\{ c_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} c_{2}\mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} c_{3}\mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal set.
(T/F) If a matrix $$U$$ has orthonormal columns, then $$UU^{T} = I$$ .
(T/F) A square matrix with orthogonal columns is an orthogonal matrix.
(T/F) If a square matrix has orthonormal columns, then it also has orthonormal rows.
(T/F) If $$W$$ is a subspace, then $$\parallel \text{proj} _{W}\mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2} + \text{∥} \mathbf{v} - \text{proj} _{W}\mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2} = \text{∥} \textbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2}$$ .

(T/F) A least-squares solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ is the vector $$A\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ in $$\text{Col} A$$ closest to $$\textbf{b}$$ , so that $$\parallel \textbf{b} - A\widehat{\textbf{x}} \parallel \leq \parallel \textbf{b} - A\textbf{x} \parallel$$ for all $$\textbf{x}$$ .
(T/F) The normal equations for a least-squares solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ are given by $$\widehat{\textbf{x}} = \left( A^{T} A)^{- 1}A^{T}{\textbf{b}} \right.$$ .

Let $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \right\}$$ be an orthonormal set. Verify the following equality by induction, beginning with $$p = 2$$ . If $$\textbf{x} = c_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}\mathbf{v}_{p}$$ , then $$\parallel \textbf{x} \parallel^{2} = \left|\right. c_{1} \left|\right.^{2} + \hdots + \left|\right. c_{p} \left|\right.^{2}$$

Let $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \right\}$$ be an orthonormal set in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Verify the following inequality, called Bessel’s inequality, which is true for each $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ :

$$\left(\parallel \mathbf{x} \parallel\right)^{2} \geq \left(\left|\right. \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{1} \left|\right.\right)^{2} + \left(\left|\right. \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{2} \left|\right.\right)^{2} + \ldots + \left(\left|\right. \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{p} \left|\right.\right)^{2}$$

section.paragraph: Exercises 33 and 34 concern the (real) Schur factorization of an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ in the form $$A = URU^{T}$$ , where $$U$$ is an orthogonal matrix and $$R$$ is an $$n \times n$$ upper triangular matrix.1

list.item: Show that if $$A$$ admits a (real) Schur factorization, $$A = URU^{T}$$ , then $$A$$ has $$n$$ real eigenvalues, counting multiplicities.

Let $$A$$ be an $$n \times n$$ matrix with $$n$$ real eigenvalues, counting multiplicities, denoted by $$\lambda_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\lambda_{n}$$ . It can be shown that $$A$$ admits a (real) Schur factorization. Parts (a) and (b) show the key ideas in the proof. The rest of the proof amounts to repeating (a) and (b) for successively smaller matrices, and then piecing together the results. Let $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ be a unit eigenvector corresponding to $$\lambda_{1}$$ , let $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{n}$$ be any other vectors such that $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{n} \right\}$$ is an orthonormal basis for $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , and then let $$U = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrrr} \mathbf{u}_{1} & \mathbf{u}_{2} & \cdots & \mathbf{u}_{n} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Show that the first column of $$U^{T}AU$$ is $$\lambda_{1}\textbf{e}_{1}$$ , where $$\textbf{e}_{1}$$ is the first column of the $$n \times n$$ identity matrix. Part (a) implies that $$U^{T} AU$$ has the form shown below. Explain why the eigenvalues of $$A_{1}$$ are $$\lambda_{2}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\lambda_{n}$$ . [Hint: See the Supplementary Exercises for Chapter 5.] $$U^{T} A U = \left[\right. \lambda_{1} & \star & \star & \star & \star 0 & & & & \vdots & & A_{1} & & 0 & & & & \left]\right.$$

[T] When the right side of an equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ is changed slightly—say, to $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b} + \text{Δ} \textbf{b}$$ for some vector $$\text{Δ} \textbf{b}$$ —the solution changes from $$\textbf{x}$$ to $$\textbf{x} + \text{Δ} \textbf{x}$$ , where $$\text{Δ} \textbf{x}$$ satisfies $$A\left( \text{Δ} \textbf{x} \right) = \text{Δ} \textbf{b}$$ . The quotient $$\parallel \text{Δ} \textbf{b} \parallel / \parallel \textbf{b} \parallel$$ is called the relative change in $$\textbf{b}$$ (or the relative error in $$\textbf{b}$$ when $$\text{Δ} \textbf{b}$$ represents possible error in the entries of $$\textbf{b}$$ ). The relative change in the solution is $$\parallel \text{Δ} \textbf{x} \parallel / \parallel \textbf{x} \parallel$$ . When $$A$$ is invertible, the condition number of $$\mathbf{\mathit{A}}$$ , written as $$\text{cond} (A)$$ , produces a bound on how large the relative change in $$\textbf{x}$$ can be:

section.paragraph: $$\frac{\parallel \Delta \mathbf{x} \parallel}{\parallel \mathbf{x} \parallel} \leq \text{cond} ( A ) \cdot \frac{\parallel \Delta \mathbf{b} \parallel}{\parallel \mathbf{b} \parallel}$$

$$T \left(\right. c \textbf{x} + d \textbf{y} \left.\right) & = [( c \textbf{x} + d \textbf{y} ) \cdot\textbf{u} ] \left(\left(\right. \textbf{u}\cdot\textbf{u} \left.\right)\right)^{- 1} \textbf{u} & = [ c (\textbf{x}\cdot\textbf{u} ) + d ( \textbf{y}\cdot\textbf{u} )] \left(\left(\right. \textbf{u}\cdot\textbf{u} \left.\right)\right)^{- 1} \textbf{u} & = c ( \textbf{x}\cdot\textbf{u} ) \left(( \textbf{u}\cdot\textbf{u} )\right)^{- 1} \textbf{u} + d ( \textbf{y}\cdot\textbf{u} ) \left(\left(\right. \textbf{u}\cdot\textbf{u} \left.\right)\right)^{- 1} \textbf{u} & = c T \left(\right. \textbf{x} \left.\right) + d T \left(\right. \textbf{y} \left.\right)$$
Thus $$T$$ is linear.

In fact, since $$\text{cond} ( A ) \times \frac{\parallel\Delta \textbf{b} \parallel}{\parallel \textbf{b} \parallel} =$$ $$23,683 \times (2.832 \times 10^{- 4}) = 6.707$$ the theoretical bound on the relative change in $$\textbf{x}$$ is $$\text{6.707}$$ (to four significant figures). This exercise shows that even when a condition number is large, the relative error in a solution need not be as large as you might expect.
